ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Brazilian participants were recruited via the [blinded for peer-review] newsletter and online social media platforms (Facebook, Instagram), and at the [blinded for peer-review].
Further, Brazilian participants were asked about their ethnic background (Black, mixed race ("pardo"), White, Indigenous, Arabic, Oriental) and in which city or state they grew up.

After selfreporting their biological sex and gender identity, observers were randomly allocated to one of the target group and attribute conditions (depending on their sex and gender; in case their sex and gender did not match, participants were excluded from further participation, to allow an unequivocal allocation to one study condition).

For example, when judging personality traits (including social skills) from faces, Asian participants were slower in their judgments, whereas Western participants were more accurate and faster, regardless of the faces' cultural background (Walker et al., 2011).

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Brazilian participants were recruited via the [blinded for peer-review] newsletter and online social media platforms (Facebook, Instagram), and at the [blinded for peer-review].

> Further, Brazilian participants were asked about their ethnic background (Black, mixed race ("pardo"), White, Indigenous, Arabic, Oriental) and in which city or state they grew up.

> After selfreporting their biological sex and gender identity, observers were randomly allocated to one of the target group and attribute conditions (depending on their sex and gender; in case their sex and gender did not match, participants were excluded from further participation, to allow an unequivocal allocation to one study condition).

> For example, when judging personality traits (including social skills) from faces, Asian participants were slower in their judgments, whereas Western participants were more accurate and faster, regardless of the faces' cultural background (Walker et al., 2011).

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Simulation-based sensitivity power analyses (1000 simulations) conducted using the package simr (Green & MacLeod, 2016) in a cross-classified multilevel model (including random intercepts for targets and observers) suggested that the smallest (116) and largest (164) target sample size would allow to detect small effect sizes of β ≥ 0.12 and β ≥ 0.10, respectively, with 80 % power at α = 0.05 (one-tailed for preregistered hypotheses, Cho & Abe, 2013; Lakens, 2016). For interaction effects in hypotheses 3-5, the power analyses yielded effect sizes of β≥0.14 to be detected with 80 % power for the smallest sample size for the interaction between observer nationality and perceived attractiveness (N = 116 Brazilian male targets, hypotheses 3-4), and of β≥0.10 for the smallest sample size for the interaction between target sex and perceived attractiveness (N = 265 Brazilian male and female targets, hypothesis 5).

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Cross-cultural perceptions of Brazilian and German men's and women's faces
table.data_collection_started: It's complicated. We have already collected some data but explain in Question 8 why readers may consider this a valid pre-registration nevertheless.
table.research_questions:
The aim of this project is to replicate various associations between social perceptions (termed halo effect, e.g., Eagly et al., 1991; Langlois et al., 2000), as well as cultural and sex differences therein, based on faces. In this section, we provide references to the studies we attempt to replicate for each hypothesised association.
We mostly expect positive associations between perceptions of positively valued attributes in line with the halo effect (i.e., perceived attractiveness is positively correlated with perceived social dominance, physical dominance, perceived prosociality, perceived health, perceived intelligence, perceived social competence, and perceived familiarity). For some of these, we hypothesise differing strengths of associations for raters from an individualistic versus a collectivistic country (here, German versus Brazilian raters), or differential associations for targets from an individualistic (Germany) versus a collectivistic country (Brazil), or by target sex and gender (male versus female; e.g., negative association between perceived attractiveness and physical dominance in women only), as specified below. 
Besides attractiveness, we hypothesise mostly positive associations amongst the other attributes based on extant empirical evidence, some of which are also qualified by rater and target cultural background as well as target sex and gender (e.g., negative association between perceived intelligence and physical dominance in women only).
Our specific hypotheses are outlined in the following:
We hypothesise positive associations of perceived facial attractiveness with perceived social dominance (Fruhen et al., 2015; Little et al., 2012; more strongly for German raters compared to Brazilian raters, judging both German and Brazilian male targets, no difference for female targets, Dion et al., 1990; Wheeler & Kim, 1997), perceived prosociality (Fruhen et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2017; more strongly for Brazilian raters compared to German raters, judging both German and Brazilian male targets, no difference for female targets, Dion et al., 1990; Wheeler & Kim, 1997), perceived health (more strongly for Brazilian raters compared to German raters, judging both German and Brazilian targets, DeBruine et al., 2010; Little et al., 2007; Penton-Voak et al., 2004), perceived intelligence (more strongly for female compared to male targets, Batres & Shiramizu, 2022), perceived social competence (Batres & Shiramizu, 2022; Eagly et al., 1991; Langlois et al., 2000; Little et al., 2012; Moore et al., 2011; Zebrowitz & Rhodes, 2004), and perceived familiarity (Batres et al., 2017; Peskin & Newell, 2004; more strongly for female compared to male targets, Kniffin & Wilson, 2004). 
We hypothesise a positive association of perceived attractiveness with perceived physical dominance for Brazilian raters and both German and Brazilian male targets (Lee et al., 2017; non-significant associations for German raters judging both German and Brazilian male targets, DeBruine et al., 2010; Little et al., 2007; Penton-Voak et al., 2004). 
We hypothesise a negative association of perceived facial attractiveness with perceived physical dominance in women (e.g., Lee et al., 2017). 
We hypothesise positive associations of perceived health with both perceived physical and social dominance for men (Boothroyd et al., 2013; for physical dominance more strongly for Brazilian raters compared to German raters, DeBruine et al., 2010; Little et al., 2007; Penton-Voak et al., 2004), and a positive association with perceived social, but not physical, dominance for women (Zebrowitz & Rhodes, 2004). 
We hypothesise positive associations of perceived prosociality with perceived health, perceived intelligence, perceived social competence, and perceived familiarity (Batres & Shiramizu, 2022; Chen et al., 2016; Little, 2014; Wentzel, 1991).
We hypothesise negative associations of perceived prosociality with perceived physical and social dominance (Chen et al., 2016; Fruhen et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2017; Little et al., 2012; Stirrat & Perrett, 2010). 
We hypothesise positive associations of perceived health with perceived intelligence (Spisak et al., 2014).
We hypothesise a positive association of perceived intelligence with perceived social competence (Batres & Shiramizu, 2022; Taborsky & Oliveira, 2012).
We hypothesise a negative association of perceived intelligence with perceived physical dominance in women (Moore et al., 2011). 
We hypothesise a positive association of perceived intelligence with perceived social competence and perceived familiarity (Batres & Shiramizu, 2022; Olivalo & Todovorv, 2010).
We hypothesise a positive association of perceived social competence with perceived familiarity (Olivalo & Todovorv, 2010). 
We hypothesise stronger interrater agreements intra- (German perceivers judging German faces and Brazilian perceivers judging Brazilian faces) than inter-culturally (German perceivers judging Brazilian faces and Brazilian perceivers judging German faces, e.g., Chen et al., 2016; Zebrowitz et al., 2012). 
We hypothesise positive correlations between ratings of German and Brazilian raters for the same faces (for perceived attractiveness, perceived physical dominance, perceived social dominance, perceived prosociality, perceived health, perceived social competence, perceived intelligence, e.g., Albright et al., 1997; Langlois et al., 2000; Zebrowitz et al., 2012), but a null-correlation for perceived familiarity (e.g., Batres et al., 2017; Peskin & Newell, 2004).
table.design_dependent_variables:
Perceived facial attractiveness (rated by German & Brazilian observers of sex different to targets’ sex, i.e., female targets rated by male observers and vice versa, groups of 10 perceivers each).
Perceived facial physical dominance (rated by same-sex German & Brazilian observers, 10 each)
Perceived facial social dominance (rated by same-sex German & Brazilian observers, 10 each)
Perceived facial prosociality (rated by same-sex German & Brazilian observers, 10 each)
Perceived facial health (rated by same-sex German & Brazilian observers, 10 each)
Perceived facial intelligence (rated by German & Brazilian observers of sex different to targets’ sex, 10 each)
Perceived facial social competence (rated by same-sex German & Brazilian observers, 10 each)
Perceived facial familiarity (rated by same-sex German & Brazilian observers, 10 each)
Items (11-point Likert scales for each):
Attractiveness: "How attractive is this man/woman?" (-5=not at all attractive, +5=very attractive) 
Physical dominance: "How likely is it that this man/woman will win a fight against another man?" ( 5=very unlikely, +5=very likely)
Social dominance: "How likely is this man/woman to tell other people what to do, to be respected, influential, and to be a leader?" ( 5=very unlikely, +5=very likely)
Prosociality: 3 items; "How trustworthy/compassionate/kind is this man/woman?" (-5=not at all trustworthy/compassionate/kind, +5=very trustworthy/compassionate/kind)
Health: "How healthy is this man/woman?" (-5=very unhealthy, +5=very healthy)
Intelligence: "How intelligent is this man/woman?" (-5=not at all intelligent, +5=very intelligent)
Social competence: "How socially competent is this man/woman?" (-5=very socially incompetent, +5=very socially competent)
Familiarity: "How familiar does this man/woman look to you?" (-5=not at all familiar, +5=very familiar)
table.study_design_overview:
- nationality of target stimuli: German vs. Brazilian targets
- sex of target stimuli: men vs. women
- nationality of raters: German vs. Brazilian raters
table.statistical_tests:
- Bivariate Pearson correlations (in case of variables’ clear deviations from normal distribution, Spearman correlations will be calculated) for bivariate associations between all rated attributes, separately for Brazilian and German targets and separately for male and female targets, as well as between Brazilian and German ratings for the same faces
- Partial correlations (e.g., inter- and intra-culturally controlling for trustworthiness (1 out of 3 prosociality items) as one main dimension of face perception, Jones et al., 2021; inter-culturally controlling for familiarity as one main influence on cross-cultural face perception, Batres et al., 2017)
- Linear regression models (including interaction terms for moderation effects; for example, for assessing differences between Brazilian and German raters for perceived social dominance for male targets: perceived facial attractiveness as DV, perceived social dominance, rater nationality and the interaction between perceived social dominance and rater nationality as IVs; for example, for assessing differences between male and female targets for perceived intelligence: perceived facial attractiveness as DV, perceived intelligence, target sex, and the interaction between perceived intelligence and target sex as IVs; plus a full multiple linear regression models with perceived facial attractiveness as the DV and the further rated attributes as IVs, separately by target nationality and rater nationality, to assess the associations of perceived attractiveness with another attribute controlling for the other attributes; multilevel linear regressions with perceived attractiveness as the DV and (target and rater) nationalities on one level and including rater nationality-target nationality interaction as a predictor, besides the other attributes hypothesised to be associated with attractiveness (each in separate models); generally these models will be run for all hypothesised associations between two attributes)
- Fisher’s r-to-z transformation for testing significance of difference in interrater agreements
- To assess findings’ robustness, the following control variables will be added calculating partial correlations or running linear regression models: target sex, target women’s and men's age, relationship status, BMI, and for cross-cultural comparisons, average temperature during ratings will be added as a potentially influential ecological factor (e.g., Jasper & Klassen, 1990; Langlois et al., 2000; Stephen & Perera, 2014; Zebrowitz & Franklin, 2014)
- Sex differences of halo effects for men versus women will be investigated using interaction terms in linear regression models
- As basic preliminary analyses, t-tests will be calculated to assess mean differences between ratings for Brazilian and German targets and between ratings from Brazilian and German raters for each attribute
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Exclusions: Rating data from raters who chose the same value for multiple consecutive photos (more than 10%) and for whom reliability analyses indicate that internal consistency for a rater group (i.e., one attribute, one set of target photos) would increase above the internal consistency’s upper limit when excluding this rater will be excluded; raters will be excluded if they indicate to be of non-male or non-female sex or gender and if the indicated gender differs from their sex (e.g., non-binary, transsexual male/female); raters and target photos will be excluded if they indicate to be bisexual or homosexual (3-6 on a 7-point Kinsey scale with endpoints 0=exclusively heterosexual to 6=exclusively homosexual, Valentova et al., 2017); facial photos will be removed from the full sample if a clear deviation from standardised posture/mimics (e.g., clear smiling, strong make-up, head turned to one side, e.g., LaFrance & Hecht, 1995) is recognisable. 
Only for German perceivers judging German targets we asked whether perceivers knew each of the targets (“Do you know this woman/man?”, 3-point response scale with 1=I don’t know him/her, 2=I know him/her a bit, 3=I know him/her well), since recent photos were and are used and no familiarity can be expected for inter-cultural ratings due to the long distance between Germany and Brazil (for the to-be-conducted ratings of German women judging the attractiveness of German men this item is not included, since German men’s photos are already ca. 8 years old, so that familiarity would be unlikely). Data points per rater and stimulus person are to be excluded for each target men or women for which a perceiver indicated a 3 (“I know him/her well”).
table.sample_size:
All stimulus photos have already been collected and prepared:
German target stimuli: N=163 men and N=155 women
Brazilian target stimuli: extant photos from four data collections between 2011 and 2019, N=119 men and N=152 women
All samples will be rated by one group per attribute by German raters. For Brazilian raters (since it is by law prohibited to pay participants in psychological studies and hence rater motivation should be lower to participate in longer studies), the samples of male and female German and of female Brazilian target stimuli will be randomly split into two to reduce rater strain (i.e., 1 group rating 82 German men, 1 group rating the remaining 81 German men, 1 group rating 78 German women, 1 group rating the remaining 77 German women, 2 groups rating 76 Brazilian women each), whereas the samples of male and female Brazilian target stimuli will be rated by one group per attributes.
Raters: 
Data are available already from n=31 German raters (having rated German men’s physical dominance, prosociality, and health)
Ratings by N=850 Brazilian and German raters (women and men) will be conducted after this preregistration has been uploaded.
Ratings will be conducted in groups of 10 (see "dependent variable"), all attributes will be rated by separate groups of raters (except for dominance and health, as in the extant data), and mean ratings will be used.
Initially, only same- OR different-sex ratings (by groups of ten raters each) will be conducted as described above (e.g., female targets’ attractiveness will be judged by 10 Brazilian and 10 German male raters, but not by female raters, whereas female target’s physical dominance will be judged by 10 Brazilian and 10 German female raters, but not by male raters; for details see “Variables”). If resources allow, further ratings will be conducted by raters of the remaining sex (i.e., attractiveness by same-sex raters, physical dominance by different-sex raters, social dominance by different-sex raters, prosociality by different-sex raters, health by different-sex raters, intelligence by same-sex raters, social competence by different-sex raters, and familiarity by different-sex raters). Hence, for all attributes we would have same- and different-sex ratings, in order to be able to assess differences and similarities between same- and different-sex ratings.
table.additional_comments:
See above (“sample size”) for exploratory analyses on remaining rater sex groups.

table.name: Cross-cultural perceptions of Brazilian and German men's and women's faces

table.title: Cross-cultural perceptions of Brazilian and German men's and women's faces
table.data_collection_started: It's complicated. We have already collected some data but explain in Question 8 why readers may consider this a valid pre-registration nevertheless.
table.research_questions:
The aim of this project is to replicate various associations between social perceptions (termed halo effect, e.g., Eagly et al., 1991; Langlois et al., 2000), as well as cultural and sex differences therein, based on faces. In this section, we provide references to the studies we attempt to replicate for each hypothesised association.
We mostly expect positive associations between perceptions of positively valued attributes in line with the halo effect (i.e., perceived attractiveness is positively correlated with perceived social dominance, physical dominance, perceived prosociality, perceived health, perceived intelligence, perceived social competence, and perceived familiarity). For some of these, we hypothesise differing strengths of associations for raters from an individualistic versus a collectivistic country (here, German versus Brazilian raters), or differential associations for targets from an individualistic (Germany) versus a collectivistic country (Brazil), or by target sex and gender (male versus female; e.g., negative association between perceived attractiveness and physical dominance in women only), as specified below. 
Besides attractiveness, we hypothesise mostly positive associations amongst the other attributes based on extant empirical evidence, some of which are also qualified by rater and target cultural background as well as target sex and gender (e.g., negative association between perceived intelligence and physical dominance in women only).
Our specific hypotheses are outlined in the following:
We hypothesise positive associations of perceived facial attractiveness with perceived social dominance (Fruhen et al., 2015; Little et al., 2012; more strongly for German raters compared to Brazilian raters, judging both German and Brazilian male targets, no difference for female targets, Dion et al., 1990; Wheeler & Kim, 1997), perceived prosociality (Fruhen et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2017; more strongly for Brazilian raters compared to German raters, judging both German and Brazilian male targets, no difference for female targets, Dion et al., 1990; Wheeler & Kim, 1997), perceived health (more strongly for Brazilian raters compared to German raters, judging both German and Brazilian targets, DeBruine et al., 2010; Little et al., 2007; Penton-Voak et al., 2004), perceived intelligence (more strongly for female compared to male targets, Batres & Shiramizu, 2022), perceived social competence (Batres & Shiramizu, 2022; Eagly et al., 1991; Langlois et al., 2000; Little et al., 2012; Moore et al., 2011; Zebrowitz & Rhodes, 2004), and perceived familiarity (Batres et al., 2017; Peskin & Newell, 2004; more strongly for female compared to male targets, Kniffin & Wilson, 2004). 
We hypothesise a positive association of perceived attractiveness with perceived physical dominance for Brazilian raters and both German and Brazilian male targets (Lee et al., 2017; non-significant associations for German raters judging both German and Brazilian male targets, DeBruine et al., 2010; Little et al., 2007; Penton-Voak et al., 2004). 
We hypothesise a negative association of perceived facial attractiveness with perceived physical dominance in women (e.g., Lee et al., 2017). 
We hypothesise positive associations of perceived health with both perceived physical and social dominance for men (Boothroyd et al., 2013; for physical dominance more strongly for Brazilian raters compared to German raters, DeBruine et al., 2010; Little et al., 2007; Penton-Voak et al., 2004), and a positive association with perceived social, but not physical, dominance for women (Zebrowitz & Rhodes, 2004). 
We hypothesise positive associations of perceived prosociality with perceived health, perceived intelligence, perceived social competence, and perceived familiarity (Batres & Shiramizu, 2022; Chen et al., 2016; Little, 2014; Wentzel, 1991).
We hypothesise negative associations of perceived prosociality with perceived physical and social dominance (Chen et al., 2016; Fruhen et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2017; Little et al., 2012; Stirrat & Perrett, 2010). 
We hypothesise positive associations of perceived health with perceived intelligence (Spisak et al., 2014).
We hypothesise a positive association of perceived intelligence with perceived social competence (Batres & Shiramizu, 2022; Taborsky & Oliveira, 2012).
We hypothesise a negative association of perceived intelligence with perceived physical dominance in women (Moore et al., 2011). 
We hypothesise a positive association of perceived intelligence with perceived social competence and perceived familiarity (Batres & Shiramizu, 2022; Olivalo & Todovorv, 2010).
We hypothesise a positive association of perceived social competence with perceived familiarity (Olivalo & Todovorv, 2010). 
We hypothesise stronger interrater agreements intra- (German perceivers judging German faces and Brazilian perceivers judging Brazilian faces) than inter-culturally (German perceivers judging Brazilian faces and Brazilian perceivers judging German faces, e.g., Chen et al., 2016; Zebrowitz et al., 2012). 
We hypothesise positive correlations between ratings of German and Brazilian raters for the same faces (for perceived attractiveness, perceived physical dominance, perceived social dominance, perceived prosociality, perceived health, perceived social competence, perceived intelligence, e.g., Albright et al., 1997; Langlois et al., 2000; Zebrowitz et al., 2012), but a null-correlation for perceived familiarity (e.g., Batres et al., 2017; Peskin & Newell, 2004).
table.design_dependent_variables:
Perceived facial attractiveness (rated by German & Brazilian observers of sex different to targets’ sex, i.e., female targets rated by male observers and vice versa, groups of 10 perceivers each).
Perceived facial physical dominance (rated by same-sex German & Brazilian observers, 10 each)
Perceived facial social dominance (rated by same-sex German & Brazilian observers, 10 each)
Perceived facial prosociality (rated by same-sex German & Brazilian observers, 10 each)
Perceived facial health (rated by same-sex German & Brazilian observers, 10 each)
Perceived facial intelligence (rated by German & Brazilian observers of sex different to targets’ sex, 10 each)
Perceived facial social competence (rated by same-sex German & Brazilian observers, 10 each)
Perceived facial familiarity (rated by same-sex German & Brazilian observers, 10 each)
Items (11-point Likert scales for each):
Attractiveness: "How attractive is this man/woman?" (-5=not at all attractive, +5=very attractive) 
Physical dominance: "How likely is it that this man/woman will win a fight against another man?" ( 5=very unlikely, +5=very likely)
Social dominance: "How likely is this man/woman to tell other people what to do, to be respected, influential, and to be a leader?" ( 5=very unlikely, +5=very likely)
Prosociality: 3 items; "How trustworthy/compassionate/kind is this man/woman?" (-5=not at all trustworthy/compassionate/kind, +5=very trustworthy/compassionate/kind)
Health: "How healthy is this man/woman?" (-5=very unhealthy, +5=very healthy)
Intelligence: "How intelligent is this man/woman?" (-5=not at all intelligent, +5=very intelligent)
Social competence: "How socially competent is this man/woman?" (-5=very socially incompetent, +5=very socially competent)
Familiarity: "How familiar does this man/woman look to you?" (-5=not at all familiar, +5=very familiar)
table.study_design_overview:
- nationality of target stimuli: German vs. Brazilian targets
- sex of target stimuli: men vs. women
- nationality of raters: German vs. Brazilian raters
table.statistical_tests:
- Bivariate Pearson correlations (in case of variables’ clear deviations from normal distribution, Spearman correlations will be calculated) for bivariate associations between all rated attributes, separately for Brazilian and German targets and separately for male and female targets, as well as between Brazilian and German ratings for the same faces
- Partial correlations (e.g., inter- and intra-culturally controlling for trustworthiness (1 out of 3 prosociality items) as one main dimension of face perception, Jones et al., 2021; inter-culturally controlling for familiarity as one main influence on cross-cultural face perception, Batres et al., 2017)
- Linear regression models (including interaction terms for moderation effects; for example, for assessing differences between Brazilian and German raters for perceived social dominance for male targets: perceived facial attractiveness as DV, perceived social dominance, rater nationality and the interaction between perceived social dominance and rater nationality as IVs; for example, for assessing differences between male and female targets for perceived intelligence: perceived facial attractiveness as DV, perceived intelligence, target sex, and the interaction between perceived intelligence and target sex as IVs; plus a full multiple linear regression models with perceived facial attractiveness as the DV and the further rated attributes as IVs, separately by target nationality and rater nationality, to assess the associations of perceived attractiveness with another attribute controlling for the other attributes; multilevel linear regressions with perceived attractiveness as the DV and (target and rater) nationalities on one level and including rater nationality-target nationality interaction as a predictor, besides the other attributes hypothesised to be associated with attractiveness (each in separate models); generally these models will be run for all hypothesised associations between two attributes)
- Fisher’s r-to-z transformation for testing significance of difference in interrater agreements
- To assess findings’ robustness, the following control variables will be added calculating partial correlations or running linear regression models: target sex, target women’s and men's age, relationship status, BMI, and for cross-cultural comparisons, average temperature during ratings will be added as a potentially influential ecological factor (e.g., Jasper & Klassen, 1990; Langlois et al., 2000; Stephen & Perera, 2014; Zebrowitz & Franklin, 2014)
- Sex differences of halo effects for men versus women will be investigated using interaction terms in linear regression models
- As basic preliminary analyses, t-tests will be calculated to assess mean differences between ratings for Brazilian and German targets and between ratings from Brazilian and German raters for each attribute
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Exclusions: Rating data from raters who chose the same value for multiple consecutive photos (more than 10%) and for whom reliability analyses indicate that internal consistency for a rater group (i.e., one attribute, one set of target photos) would increase above the internal consistency’s upper limit when excluding this rater will be excluded; raters will be excluded if they indicate to be of non-male or non-female sex or gender and if the indicated gender differs from their sex (e.g., non-binary, transsexual male/female); raters and target photos will be excluded if they indicate to be bisexual or homosexual (3-6 on a 7-point Kinsey scale with endpoints 0=exclusively heterosexual to 6=exclusively homosexual, Valentova et al., 2017); facial photos will be removed from the full sample if a clear deviation from standardised posture/mimics (e.g., clear smiling, strong make-up, head turned to one side, e.g., LaFrance & Hecht, 1995) is recognisable. 
Only for German perceivers judging German targets we asked whether perceivers knew each of the targets (“Do you know this woman/man?”, 3-point response scale with 1=I don’t know him/her, 2=I know him/her a bit, 3=I know him/her well), since recent photos were and are used and no familiarity can be expected for inter-cultural ratings due to the long distance between Germany and Brazil (for the to-be-conducted ratings of German women judging the attractiveness of German men this item is not included, since German men’s photos are already ca. 8 years old, so that familiarity would be unlikely). Data points per rater and stimulus person are to be excluded for each target men or women for which a perceiver indicated a 3 (“I know him/her well”).
table.sample_size:
All stimulus photos have already been collected and prepared:
German target stimuli: N=163 men and N=155 women
Brazilian target stimuli: extant photos from four data collections between 2011 and 2019, N=119 men and N=152 women
All samples will be rated by one group per attribute by German raters. For Brazilian raters (since it is by law prohibited to pay participants in psychological studies and hence rater motivation should be lower to participate in longer studies), the samples of male and female German and of female Brazilian target stimuli will be randomly split into two to reduce rater strain (i.e., 1 group rating 82 German men, 1 group rating the remaining 81 German men, 1 group rating 78 German women, 1 group rating the remaining 77 German women, 2 groups rating 76 Brazilian women each), whereas the samples of male and female Brazilian target stimuli will be rated by one group per attributes.
Raters: 
Data are available already from n=31 German raters (having rated German men’s physical dominance, prosociality, and health)
Ratings by N=850 Brazilian and German raters (women and men) will be conducted after this preregistration has been uploaded.
Ratings will be conducted in groups of 10 (see "dependent variable"), all attributes will be rated by separate groups of raters (except for dominance and health, as in the extant data), and mean ratings will be used.
Initially, only same- OR different-sex ratings (by groups of ten raters each) will be conducted as described above (e.g., female targets’ attractiveness will be judged by 10 Brazilian and 10 German male raters, but not by female raters, whereas female target’s physical dominance will be judged by 10 Brazilian and 10 German female raters, but not by male raters; for details see “Variables”). If resources allow, further ratings will be conducted by raters of the remaining sex (i.e., attractiveness by same-sex raters, physical dominance by different-sex raters, social dominance by different-sex raters, prosociality by different-sex raters, health by different-sex raters, intelligence by same-sex raters, social competence by different-sex raters, and familiarity by different-sex raters). Hence, for all attributes we would have same- and different-sex ratings, in order to be able to assess differences and similarities between same- and different-sex ratings.
table.additional_comments:
See above (“sample size”) for exploratory analyses on remaining rater sex groups.

We hypothesise a negative association of perceived intelligence with perceived physical dominance in women (Moore et al., 2011).
We hypothesise a positive association of perceived intelligence with perceived social competence and perceived familiarity (Batres & Shiramizu, 2022; Olivalo & Todovorv, 2010).
We hypothesise a positive association of perceived social competence with perceived familiarity (Olivalo & Todovorv, 2010).
We hypothesise stronger interrater agreements intra- (German perceivers judging German faces and Brazilian perceivers judging Brazilian faces) than inter-culturally (German perceivers judging Brazilian faces and Brazilian perceivers judging German faces, e.g., Chen et al., 2016; Zebrowitz et al., 2012).
We hypothesise positive correlations between ratings of German and Brazilian raters for the same faces (for perceived attractiveness, perceived physical dominance, perceived social dominance, perceived prosociality, perceived health, perceived social competence, perceived intelligence, e.g., Albright et al., 1997; Langlois et al., 2000; Zebrowitz et al., 2012), but a null-correlation for perceived familiarity (e.g., Batres et al., 2017; Peskin & Newell, 2004).", "Perceived facial attractiveness (rated by German & Brazilian observers of sex different to targets’ sex, i.e., female targets rated by male observers and vice versa, groups of 10 perceivers each).
Perceived facial physical dominance (rated by same-sex German & Brazilian observers, 10 each)
Perceived facial social dominance (rated by same-sex German & Brazilian observers, 10 each)
Perceived facial prosociality (rated by same-sex German & Brazilian observers, 10 each)
Perceived facial health (rated by same-sex German & Brazilian observers, 10 each)
Perceived facial intelligence (rated by German & Brazilian observers of sex different to targets’ sex, 10 each)
Perceived facial social competence (rated by same-sex German & Brazilian observers, 10 each)
Perceived facial familiarity (rated by same-sex German & Brazilian observers, 10 each)
Items (11-point Likert scales for each):
Attractiveness: \"How attractive is this man/woman?\" (-5=not at all attractive, +5=very attractive)
Physical dominance: \"How likely is it that this man/woman will win a fight against another man?\" ( 5=very unlikely, +5=very likely)
Social dominance: \"How likely is this man/woman to tell other people what to do, to be respected, influential, and to be a leader?\" ( 5=very unlikely, +5=very likely)
Prosociality: 3 items; \"How trustworthy/compassionate/kind is this man/woman?\" (-5=not at all trustworthy/compassionate/kind, +5=very trustworthy/compassionate/kind)
Health: \"How healthy is this man/woman?\" (-5=very unhealthy, +5=very healthy)
Intelligence: \"How intelligent is this man/woman?\" (-5=not at all intelligent, +5=very intelligent)
Social competence: \"How socially competent is this man/woman?\" (-5=very socially incompetent, +5=very socially competent)
Familiarity: \"How familiar does this man/woman look to you?\" (-5=not at all familiar, +5=very familiar)", "- nationality of target stimuli: German vs. Brazilian targets
- sex of target stimuli: men vs. women
- nationality of raters: German vs. Brazilian raters", "- Bivariate Pearson correlations (in case of variables’ clear deviations from normal distribution, Spearman correlations will be calculated) for bivariate associations between all rated attributes, separately for Brazilian and German targets and separately for male and female targets, as well as between Brazilian and German ratings for the same faces
- Partial correlations (e.g., inter- and intra-culturally controlling for trustworthiness (1 out of 3 prosociality items) as one main dimension of face perception, Jones et al., 2021; inter-culturally controlling for familiarity as one main influence on cross-cultural face perception, Batres et al., 2017)
- Linear regression models (including interaction terms for moderation effects; for example, for assessing differences between Brazilian and German raters for perceived social dominance for male targets: perceived facial attractiveness as DV, perceived social dominance, rater nationality and the interaction between perceived social dominance and rater nationality as IVs; for example, for assessing differences between male and female targets for perceived intelligence: perceived facial attractiveness as DV, perceived intelligence, target sex, and the interaction between perceived intelligence and target sex as IVs; plus a full multiple linear regression models with perceived facial attractiveness as the DV and the further rated attributes as IVs, separately by target nationality and rater nationality, to assess the associations of perceived attractiveness with another attribute controlling for the other attributes; multilevel linear regressions with perceived attractiveness as the DV and (target and rater) nationalities on one level and including rater nationality-target nationality interaction as a predictor, besides the other attributes hypothesised to be associated with attractiveness (each in separate models); generally these models will be run for all hypothesised associations between two attributes)
- Fisher’s r-to-z transformation for testing significance of difference in interrater agreements
- To assess findings’ robustness, the following control variables will be added calculating partial correlations or running linear regression models: target sex, target women’s and men's age, relationship status, BMI, and for cross-cultural comparisons, average temperature during ratings will be added as a potentially influential ecological factor (e.g., Jasper & Klassen, 1990; Langlois et al., 2000; Stephen & Perera, 2014; Zebrowitz & Franklin, 2014)
- Sex differences of halo effects for men versus women will be investigated using interaction terms in linear regression models
- As basic preliminary analyses, t-tests will be calculated to assess mean differences between ratings for Brazilian and German targets and between ratings from Brazilian and German raters for each attribute", "Exclusions: Rating data from raters who chose the same value for multiple consecutive photos (more than 10%) and for whom reliability analyses indicate that internal consistency for a rater group (i.e., one attribute, one set of target photos) would increase above the internal consistency’s upper limit when excluding this rater will be excluded; raters will be excluded if they indicate to be of non-male or non-female sex or gender and if the indicated gender differs from their sex (e.g., non-binary, transsexual male/female); raters and target photos will be excluded if they indicate to be bisexual or homosexual (3-6 on a 7-point Kinsey scale with endpoints 0=exclusively heterosexual to 6=exclusively homosexual, Valentova et al., 2017); facial photos will be removed from the full sample if a clear deviation from standardised posture/mimics (e.g., clear smiling, strong make-up, head turned to one side, e.g., LaFrance & Hecht, 1995) is recognisable.
Only for German perceivers judging German targets we asked whether perceivers knew each of the targets (“Do you know this woman/man?”, 3-point response scale with 1=I don’t know him/her, 2=I know him/her a bit, 3=I know him/her well), since recent photos were and are used and no familiarity can be expected for inter-cultural ratings due to the long distance between Germany and Brazil (for the to-be-conducted ratings of German women judging the attractiveness of German men this item is not included, since German men’s photos are already ca. 8 years old, so that familiarity would be unlikely). Data points per rater and stimulus person are to be excluded for each target men or women for which a perceiver indicated a 3 (“I know him/her well”).", "All stimulus photos have already been collected and prepared:
German target stimuli: N=163 men and N=155 women
Brazilian target stimuli: extant photos from four data collections between 2011 and 2019, N=119 men and N=152 women
All samples will be rated by one group per attribute by German raters. For Brazilian raters (since it is by law prohibited to pay participants in psychological studies and hence rater motivation should be lower to participate in longer studies), the samples of male and female German and of female Brazilian target stimuli will be randomly split into two to reduce rater strain (i.e., 1 group rating 82 German men, 1 group rating the remaining 81 German men, 1 group rating 78 German women, 1 group rating the remaining 77 German women, 2 groups rating 76 Brazilian women each), whereas the samples of male and female Brazilian target stimuli will be rated by one group per attributes.
Raters:
Data are available already from n=31 German raters (having rated German men’s physical dominance, prosociality, and health)
Ratings by N=850 Brazilian and German raters (women and men) will be conducted after this preregistration has been uploaded.
Ratings will be conducted in groups of 10 (see \"dependent variable\"), all attributes will be rated by separate groups of raters (except for dominance and health, as in the extant data), and mean ratings will be used.
Initially, only same- OR different-sex ratings (by groups of ten raters each) will be conducted as described above (e.g., female targets’ attractiveness will be judged by 10 Brazilian and 10 German male raters, but not by female raters, whereas female target’s physical dominance will be judged by 10 Brazilian and 10 German female raters, but not by male raters; for details see “Variables”). If resources allow, further ratings will be conducted by raters of the remaining sex (i.e., attractiveness by same-sex raters, physical dominance by different-sex raters, social dominance by different-sex raters, prosociality by different-sex raters, health by different-sex raters, intelligence by same-sex raters, social competence by different-sex raters, and familiarity by different-sex raters). Hence, for all attributes we would have same- and different-sex ratings, in order to be able to assess differences and similarities between same- and different-sex ratings.", "See above (“sample size”) for exploratory analyses on remaining rater sex groups.

table.expanded: As predicted by hypothesis 7, we found mostly positive correlations between ratings by Brazilian and German observers across attributes and target groups (all rs > .24, ps < .001; except for familiarity for male German targets as hypothesised, r = .04, p = .66; the remaining three significant positive correlations for familiarity violated hypothesis 7; see Table 3).

For male German but not Brazilian targets, there was a significant interaction term between perceived attractiveness and observer nationality on prosociality, with a significantly stronger association for German observers, contrary to hypothesis 4 (for male German targets: β = .15, SE = .07, t = 2.22, p = .03; male Brazilian targets: β = .14, SE = .07, t = 1.92, p = .056).

For Brazilian targets, there was a significant interaction on intelligence for Brazilian observers (β = .18, SE = .06, t = 2.84, p = .005, positive association for male targets, slightly negative for female targets, in line with hypothesis 5), but not for German observers (β = -.06, SE = .09, t = -0.71, p = .48).

For German targets, there were no significant interactions terms, contrary to hypothesis 5 (Brazilian observers: β = -.004, SE = .08, t = -0.05, p = .96; German observers: β = -.12, SE = .08, t = -1.55, p = .12).

For German targets, there were no significant interactions terms, contrary to hypothesis 5 (Brazilian observers: β = -.004, SE = .08, t = -0.05, p = .96; German observers: β = -.12, SE = .08, t = -1.55, p = .12).

For German targets, there was a significant interaction for Brazilian observers (β = -.31, SE = .11, t = -2.81, p = .004, significantly stronger positive association for female compared to male targets, in line with hypothesis 5), but not for German observers (β = -.09, SE = .08, t = -1.16, p = .25, contrary to hypothesis 5).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 158 columns across 12 data files.
#### Issues Identified

62 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 12 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.title: Reproducibility Check
reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 1 R code file for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  1 file skipped as byte-identical duplicate of another file already in the run (the paper links more than one repository/component).
-  0 of 1 script ran without error when executed.
-  12 installable dependencies detected.

live_data_statements: Brazilian participants were recruited via the [blinded for peer-review] newsletter and online social media platforms (Facebook, Instagram), and at the [blinded for peer-review].
Further, Brazilian participants were asked about their ethnic background (Black, mixed race ("pardo"), White, Indigenous, Arabic, Oriental) and in which city or state they grew up.

After selfreporting their biological sex and gender identity, observers were randomly allocated to one of the target group and attribute conditions (depending on their sex and gender; in case their sex and gender did not match, participants were excluded from further participation, to allow an unequivocal allocation to one study condition).

For example, when judging personality traits (including social skills) from faces, Asian participants were slower in their judgments, whereas Western participants were more accurate and faster, regardless of the faces' cultural background (Walker et al., 2011).

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 1 R code file.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1L, File = "260131_cross-cultural-comparison-attractiveness-halo-effects_clean.qmd", 
    "Runs after" = "—", Basis = "numeric"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Parsing
1 R file did not parse and cannot be run (see code_check for the errors).
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 1 script: 0 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 1 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "260131_cross-cultural-comparison-attractiveness-halo-effects_clean.qmd", 
    Outcome = "not_parsed", Detail = "", "Time (s)" = 0), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**1 script calls `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "260131_cross-cultural-comparison-attractiveness-halo-effects_clean.qmd", 
    "setwd() removed" = 1L, "Path(s) it set" = "C:/Users/kordsmeyer/ownCloud/Goettingen Postdoc/Brazil research stay 2023/Data"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```

text.text: According to the attractiveness halo effect, person perceptions are biased by physical attractiveness: More attractive people are ascribed positive attributes like competence, prosociality, and health, with cross-cultural variation.
However, extant cross-cultural studies mostly considered only in observers or targets.
This preregistered study explored nuances in attractiveness halo effects across two populations, Brazilian and German target men and women, and Brazilian and German observers.

Facial photos of 583 targets were judged separately for attractiveness, prosociality, health, intelligence, social competence, familiarity, and physical and social dominance by 565 Brazilian and 321 German observers.
Ratings between Brazilian and German observers for the same target group and attribute were positively correlated, except for familiarity for German male targets.

Attractiveness halo effects were strong (stronger for health, social competence, and familiarity compared to social dominance, prosociality, and intelligence) and mostly consistent for Brazilian and German targets and observers, with few exceptions.
Only for physical dominance, associations were mixed by target gender and nationality.
Hypotheses on cross-population and target-sex differences in halo effects were mostly unsupported.

This study supports a universality of attractiveness halo effects and contributes to a deeper understanding of variations in the halo effects of men's and women's attractiveness across two populations that differ on cultural and socioecological dimensions.
We make accurate inferences about others based on their faces in just 100 milliseconds (Willis & Todorov, 2006).

text.text: A prominent and pervasive cognitive bias in person perception is the halo effect, which holds that the impression of a person's salient attribute (e.g. physical attractiveness) unduly influences judgments of unrelated attributes (Laham & Forgas, 2022; Thorndike, 1920).

text.text: The halo effect influences different aspects of human social life and wellbeing by affecting our judgments of several attributes of our interaction partners (e.g. Hill et al., 2023; Langlois et al., 2000).

text.text: Studies demonstrated the existence of the attractiveness halo effect cross-culturally and across populations (e.g. Batres & Shiramizu, 2023).
text.formatted: Studies demonstrated the existence of the attractiveness halo effect cross-culturally and across populations (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Batres & Shiramizu, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Still, the attractiveness halo effect may differ between cultures and populations in its exact manifestation, as attributes are valued differently in more individualistic versus more collectivistic cultures.

For example, previous research has shown a stronger preference for agentic attributes, such as dominance, in individualistic cultures, and for more communal attributes, such as prosociality, in collectivistic cultures (Maeng et al., 2022; Shaffer et al., 2000; Wheeler & Kim, 1997; Zebrowitz et al., 1993).
text.formatted: For example, previous research has shown a stronger preference for agentic attributes, such as dominance, in individualistic cultures, and for more communal attributes, such as prosociality, in collectivistic cultures <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">(Maeng et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">Shaffer et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b171">Wheeler & Kim, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b178">Zebrowitz et al., 1993)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, such preferences may lead to respective attractiveness perceptions and stronger halo effects for these attributes.

However, extant studies are limited in that they rarely examined a full cross-cultural perspective, including observers and stimuli from populations differing in cultural and socioecological dimensions (e.g. Shaffer et al., 2000).

text.text: Also, the attributes for which halo effects have been investigated in earlier studies are often limited to a few attributes such as perceived trustworthiness, intelligence, and sociability (e.g. Kordsmeyer et al., 2024; Moore et al., 2011; Zebrowitz & Rhodes, 2004).
text.formatted: Also, the attributes for which halo effects have been investigated in earlier studies are often limited to a few attributes such as perceived trustworthiness, intelligence, and sociability (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Kordsmeyer et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b117">Moore et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b179">Zebrowitz & Rhodes, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: The present preregistered study offers a detailed comparison of population differences in the attractiveness halo effect on a large number of socially relevant attributes, in samples that include observers and male and female stimuli from two populations, one non-Western, more collectivistic country (Brazil) and a Western, more individualistic country (Germany, Minkov et al., 2017; Minkov & Hofstede, 2012; Santos et al., 2017), with both countries also differing substantially in their human development and well-being (World Population Review, 2026).

text.text: The halo effect describes the phenomenon that a person's salient attribute influences the perception of that person's other attributes and the overall judgement, even if there may be sufficient information to allow for independent assessment of those traits (Nisbett & Wilson, 1977).

text.text: Specifically, the perception of a person's positive attribute leads to an over-attribution of other positive attributes, even if they are unrelated to the former (Todorov et al., 2015).

text.text: As a result, the person is viewed in a "positive halo", a term first used by Thorndike (1920).

text.text: The most prominent variant of the halo effect is the attractiveness halo effect (also "What is Beautiful is Good" principle or physical attractiveness stereotype, Dion et al., 1972).

text.text: Several studies and meta-analyses have shown that observers ascribe more favourable attributes and life outcomes to attractive, compared to less attractive, targets.

Attractive individuals are perceived as more socially dominant (Feingold, 1992; Fruhen et al., 2015; Little et al., 2012), more prosocial (Fruhen et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2017), healthier (DeBruine et al., 2010; Feingold, 1992; Little et al., 2007; Penton-Voak et al., 2004), more intelligent (Batres & Shiramizu, 2023; Feingold, 1992), more socially competent (Batres & Shiramizu, 2023; Eagly et al., 1991; Langlois et al., 2000; Little et al., 2012; Moore et al., 2011; Zebrowitz & Rhodes, 2004), and more familiar (Batres et al., 2017; Peskin & Newell, 2004).
text.formatted: Attractive individuals are perceived as more socially dominant <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Feingold, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Fruhen et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">Little et al., 2012)</ref>, more prosocial <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Fruhen et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">Lee et al., 2017)</ref>, healthier <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(DeBruine et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Feingold, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">Little et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b129">Penton-Voak et al., 2004)</ref>, more intelligent <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Batres & Shiramizu, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Feingold, 1992)</ref>, more socially competent <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Batres & Shiramizu, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Eagly et al., 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">Langlois et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">Little et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b117">Moore et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b179">Zebrowitz & Rhodes, 2004)</ref>, and more familiar <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Batres et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b132">Peskin & Newell, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: On the other hand, halo effects were close to zero for integrity and concern for others (Eagly et al., 1991; Langlois et al., 2000), and heterogeneous for physical dominance (mostly positive for men and negative for women, DeBruine et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2017; Little et al., 2007; Penton-Voak et al., 2004; Rezlescu et al., 2015).

text.text: The halo effect has meaningful implications for real-life social interactions and decision-making, such that more attractive people are assumed to be more competent politicians or students (Palmer & Petersen, 2016; Talamas et al., 2016), more qualified for jobs (Verhulst et al., 2010), are more likely to receive promotions and higher salaries (Frieze et al., 1991) or more lenient court sentences (Downs & Lyons, 1991) than less attractive people.

text.text: Most research on the halo effect has been conducted on samples from Western, primarily individualistic cultures, revealing associations only in limited ways and severely limiting generalisability (Henrich et al., 2010; Laham & Forgas, 2022).

text.text: Nonetheless, the crosscultural existence of the halo effect has been shown meta-analytically (Langlois et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Nonetheless, the crosscultural existence of the halo effect has been shown meta-analytically <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">(Langlois et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: In a recent large-scale study of the cross-cultural generalisability of the attractiveness halo effect, perceived attractiveness correlated positively with most socially desirable personality traits across 45 countries in eleven world regions (Batres & Shiramizu, 2023).

text.text: Specifically, attractive male and female faces were perceived as significantly more confident, emotionally stable, intelligent, responsible, sociable, trustworthy, and less weird across all eleven world regions, and as significantly more caring and dominant, less aggressive, mean, and unhappy in some regions but not all.

Such cross-culturally stable halo effects may be explicable by both evolutionary and sociocultural factors, such as desirable physical characteristics like body symmetry, clear skin, and muscularity serving as phenotypic cues to underlying genotypic qualities, or a universal motivation to construct coherent, consistent impressions of persons, respectively (Dion et al., 1990; Laham & Forgas, 2022).

text.text: Still, there is considerable cross-cultural variation in the strength and exact manifestation of halo effects for different attributes due to differences in locally perceived violence (Borras-Guevara et al., 2017), pathogen prevalence, and mate preferences (DeBruine et al., 2010; Gangestad et al., 2006; Penton-Voak et al., 2004; Thornhill & Fincher, 2014).

text.text: For both sexes, such high-risk environments increase the value of mating partners with good genetic fitness and health, to which physical attractiveness has been proposed to be a cue.

Therefore, the association between perceived attractiveness and perceived health for both men and women should be stronger within cultures with higher pathogen prevalence and poorer public healthcare systems.

text.text: Collectivism is characterised by individuals being integrated into groups from an early age and strongly defining themselves through their relationship with others, emphasising group cohesion and loyalty (Triandis, 1999).

text.text: In a study of US white, US black, and Korean students, Zebrowitz et al. (1993) found strong agreements in ratings of attractiveness.

In combination with their findings of attractiveness halo effects differing by the associated attributes (e.g. submissiveness, warmth, honesty), the authors concluded that a general halo effect may be universal but the highly esteemed traits are not.

text.text: Hence, the ownrace effect suggests that studies investigating observers or targets from a single ethnicity can provide only limited information on cross-cultural stability and differences in halo effects.
Our preregistered study provides a broader view on cross-cultural convergence and divergence in facial judgments of socially relevant attributes.

It includes both observers and targets from two populations, Brazil and Germany, that differ on several cultural dimensions, including collectivism-individualism and human development (World Population Review, 2026).
text.formatted: It includes both observers and targets from two populations, Brazil and Germany, that differ on several cultural dimensions, including collectivism-individualism and human development <ref type="bibr">(World Population Review, 2026</ref>).

text.text: Brazil's population is more collectivistic, with a score of -56 on the individualismcollectivism dimension (factor score multiplied by 100) and a rank of 40 out of 56 countries, according to Minkov et al. (2017), and is characterised by high interdependence and a strong emphasis on familial and communal ties (Carlo et al., 2007).

(2017)</ref>, and is characterised by high interdependence and a strong emphasis on familial and communal ties <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Carlo et al., 2007</ref>).

text.text: Germany's population is more individualistic, with a score of 102 and a rank of 7 (Minkov et al., 2017), and is characterized by a stronger focus on autonomy, lower levels of interdependence (Özkarar-Gradwohl et al., 2020), and a higher degree of human development and well-being compared with Brazil (World Population Review, 2026).

text.text: These earlier findings motivated the present comparison.
At the same time, a two-country design cannot isolate individualism-collectivism from other socioecological differences between the populations.

We aimed to replicate and extend earlier findings on the attractiveness halo effect based on faces (e.g. Batres & Shiramizu, 2023; Eagly et al., 1991; Feingold, 1992; Langlois et al., 2000), focusing on cross-population and target sex differences.

text.text: As suggested by Kordsmeyer et al. (2024), our study fills a research gap by providing a more focussed cross-population perspective drawing on both observers and targets from a non-Western, more collectivistic (Brazil) and a Western, more individualistic country (Germany, Minkov et al., 2017; Pelham et al., 2022).

text.text: We offer a comprehensive approach by examining a relatively large number of socially relevant attributes, including two facets of dominance, social and physical, reflecting the multifaceted nature of dominance (e.g. Bryan et al., 2011), in contrast to earlier studies which treated dominance as a unitary construct (e.g. Batres & Shiramizu, 2023; Oosterhof & Todorov, 2008).

text.text: Based on previous findings, we investigated the following preregistered hypotheses: 1.

Perceived facial attractiveness is positively associated with perceived social dominance, perceived prosociality, perceived health, perceived intelligence, perceived social competence, and perceived familiarity.

A positive association of perceived facial attractiveness with perceived physical dominance is hypothesised in male targets judged by Brazilian observers (based on the trade-off theory; null correlation in male targets judged by German observers).
For female targets, we hypothesise a negative association of perceived facial attractiveness with perceived physical dominance.

Associations of perceived facial attractiveness with perceived health are stronger for Brazilian compared to German observers (based on a purportedly higher pathogen prevalence and poorer public healthcare system in Brazil compared to Germany, Celestino et al., 2021; Salmanton-García et al., 2025; Warnecke et al., 2020; World Health Organization, 2025a , 2025b).
text.formatted: Associations of perceived facial attractiveness with perceived health are stronger for Brazilian compared to German observers (based on a purportedly higher pathogen prevalence and poorer public healthcare system in Brazil compared to Germany, <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Celestino et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b139">Salmanton-García et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b166">Warnecke et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">World Health Organization, 2025a</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2025b)</ref>.

text.text: For male targets specifically, associations between perceived facial attractiveness and perceived prosociality are stronger for Brazilian than for German observers; for female targets, associations of perceived facial attractiveness with perceived prosociality do not differ across observers' nationalities (Dion et al., 1990; Wheeler & Kim, 1997).
text.formatted: For male targets specifically, associations between perceived facial attractiveness and perceived prosociality are stronger for Brazilian than for German observers; for female targets, associations of perceived facial attractiveness with perceived prosociality do not differ across observers' nationalities <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Dion et al., 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b171">Wheeler & Kim, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Associations of perceived facial attractiveness with perceived intelligence and perceived familiarity are stronger for female compared to male targets (Batres & Shiramizu, 2023; Kniffin et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Associations of perceived facial attractiveness with perceived intelligence and perceived familiarity are stronger for female compared to male targets <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Batres & Shiramizu, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Kniffin et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Interobserver agreements for all attributes are stronger intra-than inter-culturally (i.e. stronger for Brazilian observers judging Brazilian faces and German observers judging German faces compared to German observers judging Brazilian faces and Brazilian observers judging German faces, based on the own-race effect).

There are positive correlations between ratings by Brazilian and German observers for all attributes for the same faces, except for perceived familiarity, for which we hypothesised a null correlation.

As part of earlier studies involving further variables not relevant to this study ([blinded for peer review]), facial photographs were available from 116 Brazilian target men (age: M = 24.2 years, SD = 7.5, range 18-63, age data were unavailable for 8 men), and 149 Brazilian target women (age: M = 26.6 years, SD = 9.9, range 18-65, age data were unavailable for 9 women), 164 German target men (age: M= 24.2 years, SD = 3.2, range 18-34), and 154 German target women (age: M = 22.4 years, SD = 4.2, range 18-53).

Two facial photographs were taken of Brazilian targets while standing in front of a white or grey wall at a distance of two meters, with the participants directly facing the camera (Canon EOS T6i) with the focus set to 50mm.
They were instructed to maintain a neutral expression and wear standardised clothing.

For each German target, two facial photographs were taken while standing in front of a white wall at a distance of two meters, with the participants directly facing the camera (Canon EOS 350D) and showing a neutral facial expression.
For all targets, the more suitable of the two photos, in terms of a neutral facial expression and standardized head position, was chosen.

For Brazilian observers only, to reduce observer strain and because compensation was not possible due to legal restrictions in Brazil, the final samples of 164 German target men, 154 German target women, and 149 Brazilian female (but not the sample of 116 Brazilian male targets) were randomly divided into two sets of 82 German target men, 77 German target women, and 74-75 Brazilian target women each.
Separate groups of Brazilian observers rated these two sets, whereas German observers rated the full sets of facial photos, as outlined below.
All photos of Brazilian and German targets were delineated horizontally based on pupils (standardising for inter-pupillary distance) using WebMorph (DeBruine, 2018).

Previews of all photographs (separately for each of the four subsamples of Brazilian and German male and female targets, with each photo being displayed for 0.4 seconds one after another) were created using MiniTool MovieMaker Free (MiniTool, 2024).

text.text: Simulation-based sensitivity power analyses (1000 simulations) conducted using the package simr (Green & MacLeod, 2016) in a cross-classified multilevel model (including random intercepts for targets and observers) suggested that the smallest (116) and largest (164) target sample size would allow to detect small effect sizes of β ≥ 0.12 and β ≥ 0.10, respectively, with 80 % power at α = 0.05 (one-tailed for preregistered hypotheses, Cho & Abe, 2013; Lakens, 2016).
text.formatted: Simulation-based sensitivity power analyses (1000 simulations) conducted using the package simr <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Green & MacLeod, 2016)</ref> in a cross-classified multilevel model (including random intercepts for targets and observers) suggested that the smallest (116) and largest (164) target sample size would allow to detect small effect sizes of β ≥ 0.12 and β ≥ 0.10, respectively, with 80 % power at α = 0.05 (one-tailed for preregistered hypotheses, <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Cho & Abe, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">Lakens, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: For interaction effects in hypotheses 3-5, the power analyses yielded effect sizes of β≥0.14 to be detected with 80 % power for the smallest sample size for the interaction between observer nationality and perceived attractiveness (N = 116 Brazilian male targets, hypotheses 3-4), and of β≥0.10 for the smallest sample size for the interaction between target sex and perceived attractiveness (N = 265 Brazilian male and female targets, hypothesis 5).
A total of 893 observers from Brazil and Germany evaluated the target faces.
The Brazilian sample comprised 270 men (age: M = 36.1 years, SD = 15.5, range = 18-89) and 301 women (age: M = 38.0 years, SD = 13.7, range = 18-76).
The German sample comprised 162 men (age: M = 30.6 years, SD = 11.6, range = 19-73) and 160 women (age: M = 30.9 years, SD = 13.1, range = 19-72).
Different groups of 9-12 observers rated the faces separately for each attribute, target sex, and target nationality.

Following our preregistered procedure, we excluded overall seven individual observers (6 Brazilian men, 1 German man) whose removal increased the intraclass correlation of their group (i.e. for a given attribute and target-photo set) above the upper bound of the confidence interval.

text.text: Brazilian participants were recruited via the [blinded for peer-review] newsletter and online social media platforms (Facebook, Instagram), and at the [blinded for peer-review].
They participated voluntarily without monetary compensation due to legal restrictions in Brazil.

German observers were primarily recruited at the [blinded for peer-review] via an email newsletter for individuals interested in psychological studies and through student groups on social media platforms.
They were remunerated for their participation by monetary compensation or course credit.

Observers were only admitted to the study if they self-reported to be heterosexual (scoring 0-2 on a 7-point Kinsey scale with endpoints0 = "completely heterosexual" and6 = "completely homosexual", Kinsey et al., 1948) and cisgender (biological sex assigned at birth (female, male, or diverse) matching their gender identity (with the following response options: man, woman, nonbinary, transsexual man, transsexual woman, other); hence only participants indicating female or male as their biological sex and woman or man as their gender identity, respectively, were admitted to the study.

text.text: Further, Brazilian participants were asked about their ethnic background (Black, mixed race ("pardo"), White, Indigenous, Arabic, Oriental) and in which city or state they grew up.

This was due to large demographic heterogeneity in Brazil (Hofstede et al., 2010), which affects how familiar they are with white, more northern European looking people (southern Brazilian states such as Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina, and Paraná) or more mixed-ethnicity and black people (northern Brazilian states such as Bahia and Para) (Lins et al., 2010), and could therefore impact their perceptions of attractiveness, familiarity, and other attributes, which may in turn influence halo effects.

text.text: The rating studies were conducted online using the survey software formr.org (Arslan et al., 2020).

text.text: Targets' facial photographs were presented on computer screens.

After selfreporting their biological sex and gender identity, observers were randomly allocated to one of the target group and attribute conditions (depending on their sex and gender; in case their sex and gender did not match, participants were excluded from further participation, to allow an unequivocal allocation to one study condition).
Subsequently, they were asked to complete items on their demographics and to watch a preview of the whole subsample of photographs for a first impression of the range of all relevant faces.
Afterwards, observers viewed the photos in randomised order, one at a time, for as long as they wanted, with the rating item and response scale being shown directly underneath each photo.

All targets were judged on the following eight attributes using eleven-point Likert scales: (1) facial attractiveness by other-sex observers (i.e. female targets judged by male observers and vice versa, item: "How attractive is this man/woman?", scale endpoints -5 = "not at all attractive", +5 = "very attractive"), (2) facial physical dominance by same-sex observers (item "How likely is it that this man/woman will win a fight against another man/woman?", adapted from Puts et al., 2006; Torrance et al., 2014; Watkins et al., 2010, scale endpoints -5 = "very unlikely", +5 = "very likely"), (3) facial social dominance by same-sex observers (item "How likely is this man/woman to tell other people what to do, to be respected, influential, and to be a leader?", adapted from Puts et al., 2006; Torrance et al., 2014; Watkins et al., 2010, scale endpoints -5 = "very unlikely", +5 = "very likely"), (4) facial prosociality by same-sex observers (aggregate of three items: "How trustworthy/compassionate/kind is this man/woman?", adapted from Kogan et al., 2014, scale endpoints -5 = "not at all trustworthy/compassionate/kind", +5 = "very trustworthy/compassionate/kind"), ( 5) facial health by same-sex observers (item "How healthy is this man/woman?", scale endpoints -5 = "very unhealthy", +5 = "very healthy"), ( 6) facial intelligence by other-sex observers (item "How intelligent is this man/woman?", scale endpoints -5 = "not at all intelligent", +5 = "very intelligent"), ( 7) facial social competence by same-sex observers (item "How socially competent is this man/woman?", scale endpoints -5 = "very socially incompetent", +5 = "very socially competent"), ( 8) facial familiarity by same-sex observers (item "How familiar does this man/woman look to you?", scale endpoints -5 = "not at all familiar", +5 = "very familiar").

text.text: To increase power and based on the partly low internal consistencies (see Table 2), we ran cross-classified multilevel models (e.g. Nestler & Back, 2017) with individual ratings for physical dominance, social dominance, prosociality, health, intelligence, social competence, and familiarity nested in targets and observers, including a random intercept for target and observer (due to diverging numbers of observers between attractiveness and the other attributes, we used aggregate attractiveness ratings for each target) for hypotheses 1-5 (descriptions and results of preregistered analyses for hypotheses 1-5 based on aggregate ratings can be found in the supplement).
