text.text: To investigate the robustness of our findings, we ran partial correlations and multilevel models including the preregistered control variables target age (e.g. see Zebrowitz & Franklin, 2014), target relationship status (binary: single vs. open relationship/committed relationship/engaged/married), and target BMI.

text.text: As further control variables, we added targets' smiling (on a 3-point Likert scale with0 = "not smiling at all",1 = "slight smile", and2 = "bright smile", since smiling has been shown to influence perceptions of competence, for instance, Filkukova & Jorgensen, 2020), target men's beardedness (on a 11-point Likert scale from0 = "clean shaven" to10 = "longest, fullest beard", since beardedness is related to judgments of dominance, trustworthiness, and attractiveness, Dixson et al., 2024; Garza et al., 2024; plus there tends to be a difference in the degree of average beardedness between Brazil and European countries, Valentova, Varella, Bartova et al., 2017), as well as target women's make-up and jewellery (on a 11-point Likert scale from0 = "no make-up or jewellery" to10 = "prominent make-up and a lot of jewellery", which may especially influence perceptions of attractiveness, Mulhern et al., 2003; Schneider & Moron, 2023).

text.text: For all target groups and both observer nationalities, perceived attractiveness was positively associated with perceived prosociality, health, intelligence, social competence, and familiarity (confirming hypothesis 1).

Perceived attractiveness was positively associated with perceived intelligence for all target groups except for male Brazilian targets rated by Brazilian observers (for which we found a non-significant, yet positive association) and with perceived social dominance for all target groups except for female Brazilian targets judged by German observers (mostly in line with hypothesis 1).

Finally, for perceived physical dominance, there were significant positive associations with perceived attractiveness for male targets across populations (i.e. for Germans judging Brazilians and for Brazilians judging Germans, not significant within-nationally, for German but not Brazilian targets in line with hypothesis 2), and significant negative associations for female targets (for both target nationalities, though only for male German observers, not significant for Brazilian observers, see Table 4, partially confirming hypothesis 2).

text.text: In this study, we provide a more focussed cross-population investigation of the attractiveness halo effect and gender differences therein, based on Brazilian and German facial stimuli.

We replicated and extended earlier findings on the attractiveness halo effect (e.g. Batres & Shiramizu, 2023; Eagly et al., 1991; Langlois et al., 2000), showing mostly strong positive associations of perceived attractiveness with perceived intelligence, social competence, social dominance, prosociality, health, and familiarity (but not physical dominance) for male and female Brazilian and German targets and for Brazilian and German observers.
text.formatted: We replicated and extended earlier findings on the attractiveness halo effect (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Batres & Shiramizu, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Eagly et al., 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">Langlois et al., 2000)</ref>, showing mostly strong positive associations of perceived attractiveness with perceived intelligence, social competence, social dominance, prosociality, health, and familiarity (but not physical dominance) for male and female Brazilian and German targets and for Brazilian and German observers.

text.text: The attractiveness halo effect was found for all target groups, regardless of observer nationality (with a few exceptions for physical and social dominance, and intelligence for some target or observer groups, see Table 4).

text.text: This confirms previous findings on the general crosscultural existence of the attractiveness halo effect (Batres & Shiramizu, 2023; Langlois et al., 2000).

text.text: However, differences between observers from the two populations, one Western, more individualistic and the other non-Western, more collectivistic, did not manifest as hypothesised in this study, running counter to predictions by Wheeler and Kim (1997).
text.formatted: However, differences between observers from the two populations, one Western, more individualistic and the other non-Western, more collectivistic, did not manifest as hypothesised in this study, running counter to predictions by <ref type="bibr" target="#b171">Wheeler and Kim (1997)</ref>.

text.text: Interaction effects showed that associations were stronger for German observers in some cases, suggesting that people in Germany as a Western, more individualistic, and more developed country may generally be more susceptible to the attractiveness halo effect than those in Brazil as a non-Western, more collectivistic, and less developed country, although, as noted in the limitations, this interpretation cannot be disentangled from other differences between the two samples (e.g. socioeconomic status, urbanicity, recruitment context).

The differences could still be due to attractiveness being more important for life outcomes in individualistic cultures, as people might experience greater agency in forming relationships and consequently in other relevant life outcomes (Anderson, 2019).

text.text: Another possible explanation might be that in collectivistic countries individuals rely relatively more on the social reputation of someone than on self-inferred individual attributes.
Crucially, our findings need to be replicated in further countries differing on cultural and socioecological dimensions, to ascertain the generalisability of our results.

Concerning the gender differences in familiarity and intelligence, hypothesis 5 predicting a stronger association for female than male targets was only partly confirmed (for intelligence for Brazilian targets and Brazilian observers only, but not for German targets or German observers; for familiarity for Brazilian targets judged by German observers only).
For physical dominance, cross-population and target sex differences emerged.
For male targets, perceived attractiveness was significantly positively correlated with physical dominance for cross-population ratings (i.e.

Brazilian targets judged by German observers and German targets judged by Brazilian observers, non-significant for within-nationality ratings), only partly in line with hypothesis 2, the trade-off theory, and earlier studies within Western populations (DeBruine et al., 2010; Little et al., 2007; Penton-Voak et al., 2004).

text.text: Similarly, for perceived health, there were consistently stronger associations for German compared to Brazilian observers (for both target sexes, contrary to hypothesis 3).

While the public healthcare system and the management and treatment of pathogen risks may still be better in Germany compared to Brazil, on average, and parasitic load is higher in Brazil (Celestino et al., 2021; Salmanton-García et al., 2025; Warnecke et al., 2020; World Health Organization, 2025a , 2025b), we did not observe the hypothesised stronger positive correlation between target men's perceived attractiveness and physical dominance for Brazilian observers, but only a positive correlation for German observers.

text.text: Our results may be a peculiarity of our observer samples.

Presumably, most of the Brazilian observers who judged the target men's attractiveness and physical dominance were from the middle or upper social classes, recruited in university settings and most (68,5%) self-reported to be White (in contrast to 43,5% in the general population, Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística, 2022).
Also, most Brazilian observers were from the cities of Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro, which are economically superior to most other regions in Brazil.
This means that the generally higher pathogen prevalence and poorer healthcare system in Brazil may have been less relevant to the majority of our observer samples.
These potential explanations should be investigated further in follow-up studies.

Alternatively, in a re-analysis of the data from Debruine et al. (2010), Brooks et al. (2011) showed that rather than a national health index, women's preferences for masculinity were better explained by a country's income equality (see also Jones et al., 2021 and Lee et al., 2025 for further evidence conflicting with trade-off theory).

text.text: This might explain why we did not find associations with judgments of physical dominance and health as predicted by trade-off theory, since our Brazilian observer samples were mainly composed of participants from the economically more developed cities of Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro.

text.text: In our study, the more communal and affiliative attribute prosociality and social competence were not more strongly associated with perceived attractiveness for observers from a non-Western, more collectivistic, less developed compared to those from a Western, more individualistic, and more developed country.

The smaller correlation for Brazilian observers could reflect cultural norms related to the stronger collectivism in Brazil, in that prosociality is considered a baseline trait, which is taken as given and people may not differ as much in their willingness to exhibit or expect prosocial behaviours as people in individualistic countries (see Levine et al., 2001 for experimental evidence of highest degrees of helping behaviour in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, compared to 22 cities in other countries).
text.formatted: The smaller correlation for Brazilian observers could reflect cultural norms related to the stronger collectivism in Brazil, in that prosociality is considered a baseline trait, which is taken as given and people may not differ as much in their willingness to exhibit or expect prosocial behaviours as people in individualistic countries (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">Levine et al., 2001</ref> for experimental evidence of highest degrees of helping behaviour in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, compared to 22 cities in other countries).

text.text: Hence, prosociality appears to be seen as more independent from appearance in Brazil (also evidenced by the non-significant correlation for female German targets and small positive correlation for female Brazilian targets, both for Brazilian observers).
The mostly stronger association of attractiveness with prosociality in Germany may be explicable by a more individualistic cultural orientation.

A speculative post-hoc explanation may come from studies which showed that people from individualistic countries are more likely to rely on superficial cues such as physical appearance (e.g. facial features and linked attractiveness) in social judgments.

For example, when judging personality traits (including social skills) from faces, Asian participants were slower in their judgments, whereas Western participants were more accurate and faster, regardless of the faces' cultural background (Walker et al., 2011).

text.text: Moreover, people in individualistic cultures tend to frame relationships more strongly in terms of physical attractiveness, choosing friends and partners based on personal preferences and as a form of self-expression (Anderson et al., 2008).

text.text: In contrast, people in more collectivistic cultures emphasise interdependence and embeddedness within family and community structures, with attractiveness playing a minor role.
Our study is broadly consistent with, at least for evaluations of women, though this interpretation should be treated cautiously given the limitations of a two-country comparison.

text.text: Although our study supports previous findings of robust, positive attractiveness halo effects (e.g. Batres & Shiramizu, 2023; Langlois et al., 2000), effect sizes varied by attribute.

text.text: Attractiveness halo effects were strongest for perceived health, social competence, and (somewhat surprisingly) familiarity, and smaller for prosociality, intelligence, and especially for social and physical dominance, with some effects even going in the opposite direction for the latter two.
This pattern of results was similar, however, to those found in a meta-analysis including mostly Western studies by Eagly et al. (1991).
text.formatted: This pattern of results was similar, however, to those found in a meta-analysis including mostly Western studies by <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Eagly et al. (1991)</ref>.

text.text: Their meta-analysis showed largest effects for social competence, intermediate for potency and intellectual competence, and nearzero effects for concern for others, which are comparable to our attributes social/physical dominance, intelligence, and prosociality, respectively.

Effect sizes in our study were largely comparable to those in the cross-cultural study by Batres and Shiramizu (2023), though overall smaller, particularly for physical dominance, which might be explained by the dominance item used.

text.text: Finally, interobserver agreements (ICCs) were not significantly larger for Brazilian observers judging Brazilian faces and German observers judging German faces compared to German observers judging Brazilian faces and Brazilian observers judging German faces.
These results run counter to earlier results (e.g. Zebrowitz et al., 2012), the own-race effect (Tanaka et al., 2004), and our hypothesis 6.

text.text: Such non-significant differences may be explicable by clearly stronger variation in cultural values within countries rather than between countries (Taras et al., 2016), especially in culturally, demographically, economically, and ecologically heterogeneous Brazil (Hofstede et al., 2010; Torres et al., 2015).

text.text: However, our Brazilian observer sample was comparably homogenous, with 68,5% identifying as White, 21,4% as Brown, and only 10,1% as either Arabic, Black, Oriental, or Indigenous.
Still, influences of cultural values should be explored further in halo effect research.

Our findings underline the meaningful implications of the attractiveness halo effect for social interaction, social life, and well-being. Langlois et al. (2000) conducted a meta-analysis showing that attractive children and adults are not only judged but also treated more positively than unattractive children and adults, even beyond zero-acquaintance interactions.

text.text: These attractiveness biases spill over to numerous aspects of social and societal life.

Attractive individuals, relative to more unattractive individuals, experience advantages in dating contexts (e.g. Eastwick et al., 2011), educational contexts (Abikoff et al., 1993; Dennis, 2007; Schmidt et al., 2023), on the labour market (Hosoda et al., 2003; Maestripieri et al., 2017), in politics (Olivola & Todorov, 2010; Palmer & Peterson, 2016), in health treatments (Martin et al., 1977; Napoleon et al., 1980), in court (Efran, 1974; Zebrowitz & McDonald, 1991), and regarding psychological well-being (Umberson & Hughes, 1987).
text.formatted: Attractive individuals, relative to more unattractive individuals, experience advantages in dating contexts (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Eastwick et al., 2011)</ref>, educational contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abikoff et al., 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Dennis, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b142">Schmidt et al., 2023)</ref>, on the labour market <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Hosoda et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">Maestripieri et al., 2017)</ref>, in politics <ref type="bibr" target="#b122">(Olivola & Todorov, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b126">Palmer & Peterson, 2016)</ref>, in health treatments <ref type="bibr" target="#b111">(Martin et al., 1977;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b119">Napoleon et al., 1980)</ref>, in court <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Efran, 1974;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b177">Zebrowitz & McDonald, 1991)</ref>, and regarding psychological well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b160">(Umberson & Hughes, 1987)</ref>.

text.text: Attractive individuals are also preferred in social interactions and gatherings, and hence have better chances of developing more social capital than less attractive individuals (Palmer & Peterson, 2021).
text.formatted: Attractive individuals are also preferred in social interactions and gatherings, and hence have better chances of developing more social capital than less attractive individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b127">(Palmer & Peterson, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, not all social implications are positive, as higher facial femininity in women (as a proxy of attractiveness) may elicit stronger jealousy in mating rivals (Dong et al., 2025), and attractive individuals are thought of as less good parents compared to average-looking individuals (Cash & Duncan, 1984; Dion et al., 1972; bear in mind that these are rather dated findings which may have been based on now outdated stereotypes).

text.text: On the other hand, less attractive individuals may face disadvantages due to their perceived unattractiveness, called negative halo effect, devils effect, or horns effect (Cook et al., 2003; Griffin & Langlois, 2006; Kordsmeyer et al., 2026; Radeke & Stahelski, 2020).
text.formatted: On the other hand, less attractive individuals may face disadvantages due to their perceived unattractiveness, called negative halo effect, devils effect, or horns effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Cook et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Griffin & Langlois, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">Kordsmeyer et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b135">Radeke & Stahelski, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, while all attributes in this study were positively framed and connotated (except possibly physical dominance), future research should investigate negatively framed attributes and social consequences of low attractiveness in greater depth.

Despite the relatively strong attractiveness halo effects and their meaningful implications for person perception and social interactions, it is unclear whether face perceptions are valid predictors of individual characteristics and behaviour, or if the halo effect is primarily a cognitive bias resulting in invalid stereotypes.
Investigations of actual associations of attractiveness with intelligence yielded mixed results (Breil et al., 2021; Driebe et al., 2021; Feingold, 1992; Mitchem et al., 2015; Kanazawa, 2011).

text.text: A methodological clarification is warranted.

Classically, the attractiveness halo effect refers to an intra-observer bias in which one observer's judgment of attractiveness influences their evaluations of other attributes of the same target (Dion et al., 1972; Thorndike, 1920).
text.formatted: Classically, the attractiveness halo effect refers to an intra-observer bias in which one observer's judgment of attractiveness influences their evaluations of other attributes of the same target <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Dion et al., 1972;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b151">Thorndike, 1920)</ref>.

text.text: Our design, using independent observer groups per attribute, yields between-group correlations and cannot isolate this pure intra-individual component from shared facial-cue covariation.
This approach is nevertheless standard and is routinely labelled the "attractiveness halo effect".

Meta-analyses define the phenomenon as the consensual association between rated attractiveness and positive attributes, regardless of whether the same individuals supplied both ratings (Eagly et al., 1991; Langlois et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Meta-analyses define the phenomenon as the consensual association between rated attractiveness and positive attributes, regardless of whether the same individuals supplied both ratings <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Eagly et al., 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">Langlois et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Recent large-scale studies employing independent or randomly assigned observers per attribute interpret the resulting correlations identically (Batres & Shiramizu, 2023; Kordsmeyer et al., 2024; Kordsmeyer et al., 2026; Talamas et al., 2016).

text.text: One central limitation of the present study is that it only encompassed observers from two countries, one European and one South American.

To increase the generalisability of our findings, our study should be replicated in further countries varying on cultural and socioecological dimensions like individualism-collectivism (cf. Minkov et al., 2017), including both targets and observers from these countries.
text.formatted: To increase the generalisability of our findings, our study should be replicated in further countries varying on cultural and socioecological dimensions like individualism-collectivism (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">Minkov et al., 2017)</ref>, including both targets and observers from these countries.

text.text: Moreover, data in both countries were collected predominantly in university settings.

University-educated participants, especially those from major urban centres such as São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro in Brazil, may share more similar values, norms, and cognitive styles than the broader national populations, potentially attenuating the cultural distance the study aimed to examine.

Besides the attributes investigated in this study, further attributes crucially relevant to social interactions and hence to person perception should be investigated regarding possible cross-cultural nuances in attractiveness halo effects, such as warmth, emotional stability, confidence, or happiness (e.g. Batres & Shiramizu, 2023; Fiske et al., 2007).

text.text: These and similar attributes have been examined for potential halo effects, albeit seldom with a full cross-cultural perspective for stimuli and observers (cf. Batres & Shiramizu, 2023).

text.text: A further limitation concerns the use of facial photos to assess perceptions of socially relevant attributes.

Although a recent meta-analysis demonstrated ecological validity of photobased attractiveness judgments (Kaschel & Hildebrandt, 2023) and the face is a central source of social information (Currie & Little, 2009), these static facial stimuli capture only a proportion of socially relevant cues.

text.text: Hence, future studies should include additional modalities, such as vocal and olfactory stimuli (Demattè et al., 2007; Kordsmeyer et al., 2020; Pereira, Varella et al., 2019; Saxton et al., 2009; Trebicky et al., 2023), as well as bodily stimuli (Kordsmeyer et al., 2024; Pereira, Silva et al., 2019).

text.text: Furthermore, contemporarily popular beautification or appearance enhancement strategies reportedly augment perceived attractiveness, such as in social media or using makeup or plastic surgery, but distort typical associations with other socially relevant attributes.
For example, Liang et al. (2023) showed that women's faces after plastic surgery were perceived as more trustworthy and more attractive than natural faces or faces wearing makeup.

text.text: However, when observers were informed about the plastic surgery, trustworthiness judgments declined considerably.

In another study, minimally invasive facial aesthetic treatment led to a small, but significant increase in perceived attractiveness (especially as a short-term, but not as a long-term partner), but not in trustworthiness (Jaeger et al., 2025).

text.text: Further, attractiveness halo effects on perceived intelligence and trustworthiness were still detected after applying an AI-based beauty filter to facial photos rendering the faces more attractive.
However, they were weaker compared to effects for the original faces (Gulati et al., 2024).

text.text: In our study, we had no knowledge of any plastic surgery, but coded female targets' makeup and male targets' beardedness.
Controlling for these factors, associations of attractiveness with the other attributes remained mostly unchanged.

Bivariate associations between Brazilian and German target men's beardedness and attractiveness were close to zero and non-significant (in line with Dixon & Vasey, 2012; in contrast to Dixson & Brooks, 2013; Dixson et al., 2016).

Possible interpretations for the latter include a stronger naturalness preference for German men judging Brazilian women or cultural differences in evaluation of the targets' makeup (Cunningham et al., 1995; Etcoff et al., 2011).

text.text: However, it needs to be kept in mind that the association between makeup and attractiveness was positive for German target women.

Because makeup was not experimentally manipulated, the association may also reflect unmeasured characteristics correlated with makeup, such as self-presentation style, or other facial and contextual cues (Penton-Voak et al., 2004).

text.text: So far, most research on halo effects has focused exclusively on associations on the side of targets and stimuli.
In this study, we analysed individual ratings in cross-classified multilevel models that included random intercepts for targets and observers (and, where relevant, observer nationality).

Although the multilevel models account for individual differences in overall scale use via observer random intercepts, cultural differences in response style (e.g. extreme versus central tendency) between Brazilian and German observers could still affect mean-level comparisons (Table 3) and, potentially, correlational patterns.
text.formatted: Although the multilevel models account for individual differences in overall scale use via observer random intercepts, cultural differences in response style (e.g. extreme versus central tendency) between Brazilian and German observers could still affect mean-level comparisons (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref>) and, potentially, correlational patterns.

text.text: Future work could more explicitly model extreme response style to further rule out this alternative explanation.

Further, while these models account for overall observer-level variance, they do not examine specific inter-individual differences in cognitive and personality-related characteristics, which likely strongly influence person perception, including halo effects.
First, in our study we employed groups of either other-sex or same-sex observers, depending on the attribute.

Specifically, only for attractiveness and intelligence (attributes prominent in mate choice) observer sex converged, whereas for the other attributes observer sex (same-sex judgments due to their relevance in intrasexual competition) differed from attractiveness.
This divergence may complicate the comparability of the strength of halo effects, given that earlier studies showed that observer sex affects judgments of attractiveness (Marcus & Miller, 2003).

text.text: These measures should be investigated further for a more complete understanding of cross-cultural nuances in halo effects and mechanisms of person perception generally.
This study extends earlier findings on cross-population nuances of the attractiveness halo effect based on faces as a persistent cognitive bias in person perception.

Overall, associations with the perceived attractiveness of several socially relevant attributes were similar for observers from a non-Western, more collectivistic, less developed country (Brazil) as for observers from a Western, more individualistic, more developed country (Germany), and for both male and female targets.
Consistently positive correlations were found for health, social competence, and unexpectedly familiarity, and mostly positive correlations for social dominance, prosociality, and intelligence.
In contrast, associations were mixed for physical dominance by target gender and nationality.
In conclusion, this study demonstrates very similar perceptions across the two populations for a range of socially relevant attributes.
Thus, only limited cross-population differences in halo effects in our study mostly run counter to hypotheses based on earlier theoretical and empirical suggestions.
These findings add to our understanding of biases in person perception and why more positive social outcomes are often experienced by more attractive people.

text.text: For each observer group (separately for target sex, target nationality, observer nationality, and attribute), ratings were aggregated and mean values were used in further analyses.
As preregistered, preliminary analyses used t-tests to assess mean differences in ratings between Brazilian and German observers for each attribute and target group.

Pearson correlations were calculated to examine bivariate associations of perceived attractiveness with perceived physical dominance, social dominance, prosociality, health, intelligence, social competence, and familiarity.

Linear regression models were run for moderator effects of observer nationality (hypotheses 3-4) or target sex (hypothesis 5) (with perceived attractiveness and either observer nationality or target sex as the predictor variables plus their interaction term, and a second attribute as the outcome variable).
As preregistered, one-sided tests were used for directional hypotheses (Cho & Abe, 2013; Lakens, 2016).
text.formatted: As preregistered, one-sided tests were used for directional hypotheses <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Cho & Abe, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">Lakens, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: To investigate the robustness of our findings, we ran partial correlations and linear regression models including the preregistered control variables target age (e.g. see Zebrowitz & Franklin, 2014), target relationship status (binary: single vs. open relationship/committed relationship/engaged/married), and target BMI.
text.formatted: To investigate the robustness of our findings, we ran partial correlations and linear regression models including the preregistered control variables target age (e.g. see <ref type="bibr" target="#b175">Zebrowitz & Franklin, 2014)</ref>, target relationship status (binary: single vs. open relationship/committed relationship/engaged/married), and target BMI.

text.text: As further control variables, we added targets' smiling, target men's beardedness, as well as target women's make-up and jewellery.
Furthermore, the strength of associations between Brazilian and German observers on the same attributes were compared employing moderation analyses in regression models.
Bivariate Pearson correlations of attractiveness with all other attributes are shown in Table S1, stratified by target group and observer nationality.
text.formatted: Bivariate Pearson correlations of attractiveness with all other attributes are shown in Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>, stratified by target group and observer nationality.

text.text: For all target groups and both observer nationalities, perceived attractiveness correlated positively with perceived health, social competence, and familiarity (confirming hypothesis 1).

Perceived attractiveness correlated positively with perceived intelligence for all target groups except for male Brazilian targets rated by Brazilian observers (for which we found a non-significant, yet positive association), with perceived prosociality for all target groups except for female German targets judged by Brazilian observers, and with perceived social dominance for all target groups except for female Brazilian targets judged by German observers (mostly in line with hypothesis 1).

Finally, for perceived physical dominance, there were significant positive correlations with perceived attractiveness for male targets (for both target nationalities, only for male German but not Brazilian observers, contrary to hypothesis 2), and significant negative correlations for female targets (again for both target nationalities, though only for male German but not Brazilian observers, see Table S1, partially confirming hypothesis 2).
text.formatted: Finally, for perceived physical dominance, there were significant positive correlations with perceived attractiveness for male targets (for both target nationalities, only for male German but not Brazilian observers, contrary to hypothesis 2), and significant negative correlations for female targets (again for both target nationalities, though only for male German but not Brazilian observers, see Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>, partially confirming hypothesis 2).

text.text: Almost all correlations remained virtually unchanged when controlling for age, smiling, make-up, glasses, beardedness, and the headband worn by Brazilian targets (see Table S2).

To test hypotheses 3 to 5 on cross-cultural and sex differences, linear regression models were run including interaction terms between perceived attractiveness and observer nationality (hypotheses 3-4) or target sex (hypothesis 5) predicting a second attribute.

For all four target group, the association between perceived attractiveness and health was significantly stronger for German compared to Brazilian observers (contrary to hypothesis 3, interaction term for male Brazilian targets: β = .25, SE = .07, t = 3.43, p < .001; interaction term for female Brazilian targets: β = .22, SE = .08, t = 2.95, p = .003; interaction term for male German targets: β = .30, SE = .09, t = 3.19, p = .002; interaction term for female German targets: β = .25, SE = .08, t = 2.90, p = .004).
text.formatted: For all four target group, the association between perceived attractiveness and health was significantly stronger for German compared to Brazilian observers (contrary to hypothesis 3, interaction term for male Brazilian targets: β = .25, SE = .07, t = 3.43, p < .001; interaction term for female Brazilian targets: β = .22, SE = .08, t = 2.95, p = .003; interaction term for male German targets: β = .30, SE = .09, t = 3.19, p = .002; interaction term for female German targets: β = .25, SE = .08, t = 2.90, p = .004).

text.text: For male German but not Brazilian targets, there was a significant interaction term between perceived attractiveness and observer nationality on prosociality, with a significantly stronger association for German observers, contrary to hypothesis 4 (for male German targets: β = .15, SE = .07, t = 2.22, p = .03; male Brazilian targets: β = .14, SE = .07, t = 1.92, p = .056).

For female targets, there were significant interactions on prosociality for Brazilian targets (β = .37, SE = .09, t = 4.05, p < .001) and German targets (β = .18, SE = .06, t = 2.84, p = .005), with a positive association for German observers and a negative association for Brazilian observers, contrary to our hypothesis 4.
text.formatted: For female targets, there were significant interactions on prosociality for Brazilian targets (β = .37, SE = .09, t = 4.05, p < .001) and German targets (β = .18, SE = .06, t = 2.84, p = .005), with a positive association for German observers and a negative association for Brazilian observers, contrary to our hypothesis 4.

text.text: For Brazilian targets, there was a significant interaction on intelligence for Brazilian observers (β = .18, SE = .06, t = 2.84, p = .005, positive association for male targets, slightly negative for female targets, in line with hypothesis 5), but not for German observers (β = -.06, SE = .09, t = -0.71, p = .48).

For German targets, there were no significant interactions terms, contrary to hypothesis 5 (Brazilian observers: β = -.004, SE = .08, t = -0.05, p = .96; German observers: β = -.12, SE = .08, t = -1.55, p = .12).

For familiarity, there were significant interactions for Brazilian targets and both Brazilian observers (β = .29, SE = .09, t = 3.41, p < .001, positive association for male targets, slightly negative for female targets, contrary to hypothesis 5) and German observers (β = -.25, SE = .09, t = -2.87, p = .004, significantly stronger positive association for female compared to male targets, in line with hypothesis 5).
text.formatted: For familiarity, there were significant interactions for Brazilian targets and both Brazilian observers (β = .29, SE = .09, t = 3.41, p < .001, positive association for male targets, slightly negative for female targets, contrary to hypothesis 5) and German observers (β = -.25, SE = .09, t = -2.87, p = .004, significantly stronger positive association for female compared to male targets, in line with hypothesis 5).

text.text: For German targets, there was a significant interaction for Brazilian observers (β = -.31, SE = .11, t = -2.81, p = .004, significantly stronger positive association for female compared to male targets, in line with hypothesis 5), but not for German observers (β = -.09, SE = .08, t = -1.16, p = .25, contrary to hypothesis 5).

For robustness checks, as preregistered, linear regression models were run with perceived attractiveness as the dependent variable and observer nationality and a second attribute as the two independent variables plus their interaction terms.

First, there was no significant interaction for perceived health for male or female Brazilian targets (male targets: β = .13, SE = .14, t = 0.92, p = .36; female targets: β = -.03, SE = .08, t = -0.35, p = .73; both different from significant interaction with attractiveness as independent variable but still contrary to hypothesis 3), but only for male German targets (β = .25, SE = .10, t = 2.44, p = .02, stronger positive for German observers than for Brazilian observers, similar as with attractiveness as independent variable and still contrary to hypothesis 3; non-significant for female German targets: β = .05, SE = .11, t = 0.40, p = .69, different from significant interaction with attractiveness as independent variable but still contrary to hypothesis 3).

Second, for prosociality, there was only one significant interaction (for female Brazilian targets: β = .48, SE = .19, t = 2.52, p = .01, positive association for German observers and negative association for Brazilian observers, similar as with attractiveness as independent variable but still contrary to hypothesis 4; male Brazilian targets: β = -.06, SE = .22, t = -0.25, p = .80, similar as with attractiveness as independent variable but still contrary to hypothesis 4; male German targets: β = .04, SE = .16, t = 0.26, p = .80; female German targets: β = .27, SE = .14, t = 1.90, p = .058, for the latter two different from significant interactions with attractiveness as independent variable but still contrary to hypothesis 4).

For Brazilian targets, there was a significant interaction on intelligence for Brazilian observers (β = -.96, SE = .19, t = -5.09, p < .001, stronger positive association for female than for male targets, different from significant interaction in opposite direction with attractiveness as independent variable and now contrary to hypothesis 5) and for German observers (β = -.41, SE = .12, t = -3.44, p < .001, stronger positive association for female than for male targets, different from non-significant interaction with attractiveness as independent variable, still contrary to hypothesis 5).

text.text: For German targets, there was a significant interaction for German observers (β = -.24, SE = .11, t = -2.31, p = .02, stronger positive association for female than for male targets, different from non-significant interaction with attractiveness as independent variable, still contrary to hypothesis 5), but not Brazilian observers (β = -.19, SE = .15, t = -1.27, p = .22, similar to non-significant interaction with attractiveness as independent variable and still contrary to hypothesis 5).

For familiarity, there were significant interactions for Brazilian targets and German observers (β = -.37, SE = .11, t = -3.32, p = .001, stronger positive association for female compared to male targets, similar to significant interaction with attractiveness as independent variable and still in line with hypothesis 5; non-significant for Brazilian observers: β = .20, SE = .16, t = 1.30, p = .20, different from significant interaction with attractiveness as independent variable but still contrary to hypothesis 5) as well as for German targets (Brazilian observers: β = -.25, SE = .10, t = -2.41, p = .02, stronger positive association for female than for male targets, different from non-significant interaction with attractiveness as independent variable, but now in line with hypothesis 5; German observers: β = .44, SE = .09, t = 4.79, p < .001, stronger positive for male targets, different from nonsignificant interaction with attractiveness as independent variable and still contrary to hypothesis 5).
